content: 1. Anaphylaxis and hypersensitivity reactions have been reported with the use of antibacterial agents, including daptomycin (CUBICIN). These reactions can be life-threatening. If an allergic reaction occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate medical therapy should be initiated. 2. Myopathy, characterized by muscle pain or weakness accompanied by elevations in creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels exceeding 10 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), has been observed in patients receiving daptomycin. Cases of rhabdomyolysis, with or without acute renal failure, have also been reported. Patients on daptomycin should be monitored for muscle pain or weakness, particularly in the distal extremities. Weekly CPK monitoring is recommended, with more frequent monitoring in patients who are on or have recently used HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors or those who develop elevated CPK levels during treatment. In patients with renal impairment, both renal function and CPK levels should be monitored more frequently than once weekly. Studies have shown that CPK elevations are more common when daptomycin is administered more than once daily; therefore, dosing should not exceed once daily. Daptomycin should be discontinued in patients with unexplained symptoms of myopathy and CPK levels greater than 1,000 U/L (approximately 5× ULN) or in asymptomatic patients with CPK levels exceeding 2,000 U/L (≥10× ULN). Additionally, consideration should be given to temporarily discontinuing other agents associated with rhabdomyolysis, such as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, in patients receiving daptomycin. 3. Eosinophilic pneumonia has been reported in patients treated with daptomycin. Symptoms include fever, shortness of breath with hypoxic respiratory insufficiency, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. This condition typically develops 2 to 4 weeks after starting daptomycin and resolves upon discontinuation of the drug and initiation of systemic corticosteroid therapy. Patients presenting with these symptoms should undergo immediate medical evaluation, and daptomycin should be discontinued promptly. Treatment with systemic steroids is recommended. 4. Cases of peripheral neuropathy have been reported in patients receiving daptomycin during postmarketing surveillance. Physicians should remain vigilant for signs and symptoms of peripheral neuropathy in patients undergoing treatment with this drug. 5. Clostridium difficile–associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all systemic antibacterial agents, including daptomycin. CDAD can range in severity from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial therapy disrupts the normal flora of the colon, allowing overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and could require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibacterial use, even if it occurs more than two months after treatment. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibacterial therapy not directed against C. difficile may be necessary. Management should include appropriate fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibacterial therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation as clinically indicated. 6. In cases of persistent or relapsing Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia or endocarditis, or in patients with poor clinical response, repeat blood cultures should be performed. If S. aureus is detected, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) susceptibility testing should be conducted using standardized methods. Diagnostic evaluation should be performed to identify potential sequestered infection sites. Appropriate surgical interventions, such as debridement, removal of prosthetic devices, or valve replacement surgery, may be required. A change in antibacterial regimen should also be considered. Treatment failure in these cases may be associated with reduced susceptibility to daptomycin, as indicated by increasing MIC values for the S. aureus isolate. 7. Limited data are available regarding the clinical efficacy of daptomycin in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <50 mL/min). In Phase 3 trials for complicated skin and skin structure infections (cSSSI), only a small percentage of patients had baseline creatinine clearance <50 mL/min. Subgroup analysis of the Phase 3 S. aureus bacteremia/endocarditis trial revealed lower clinical success rates in patients with baseline creatinine clearance <50 mL/min when treated with daptomycin. This decrease in efficacy was not observed in comparator-treated patients. These findings should be considered when selecting antibacterial therapy for patients with moderate to severe renal impairment. 8. Daptomycin has been observed to cause a significant concentration-dependent false prolongation of prothrombin time (PT) and elevation of the International Normalized Ratio (INR) when certain recombinant thromboplastin reagents are used in laboratory assays. This interaction should be taken into account when interpreting coagulation test results in patients receiving daptomycin. 9. The use of antibacterial agents, including daptomycin, may promote the overgrowth of non-susceptible microorganisms. Prescribing daptomycin in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria.
